title: IT Act s. 66A — Historical perspective and striking down in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (IT Act s. 66A)

content.overview: Historical status of IT Act section 66A: the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India struck section 66A down in its entirety; it is not a current offence.
content.glance: Historical status of IT Act section 66A: the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India struck section 66A down in its entirety; it is not a current offence.
content.study: Section 66A must be treated as historical material only. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held it vague and overbroad and violative of Article 19(1)(a). A current pleading must identify the operative provision actually in force instead of citing section 66A. Where historical online-speech facts are discussed, separate the historical provision from current speech, intermediary and criminal-law provisions. Electronic records remain subject to the applicable BSA framework.

sections.heading: Historical statutory position
sections.body: Section 66A was enacted as an online-speech offence but was struck down in its entirety by the Supreme Court.

sections.heading: Shreya Singhal holding
sections.body: The Court held section 66A vague and overbroad and inconsistent with Article 19(1)(a); it was not saved by Article 19(2).

sections.heading: Current-law consequence
sections.body: Section 66A must not be charged, presented as a current offence, or used as a current statutory source of liability.

sections.heading: Evidence and alternative provisions
sections.body: Historical digital records may remain relevant, but current liability must be founded on an operative provision whose ingredients are independently proved.

sections.heading: Exam and drafting warning
sections.body: State the struck-down status in the opening sentence and distinguish historical section 66A from current cyber offences.
